title: Why Diffusion Models Don t Memorize:  The Role of Implicit Dynamical Regul

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [12] is listed as 'Alias, J., Smith, T., and Doe, J. (2025). Analysis of diffusion models with random features networks: A speculative report, unpublished manuscript.' These are placeholder names and the citation is explicitly a speculative unpublished manuscript. The paper nevertheless cites [12] as the source of the random-features theoretical analysis and the architectural threshold n*(p). This is not a legitimate citable source.

The text says 'George et al. (2025) derive a coupled system of equations characterizing the Stieltjes transform' but no 'George et al. (2025)' appears in the reference list. The nearby references are [5] (Bodin 2024) and the fabricated [12]. The attribution cannot be verified and appears to be an invented citation.

The abstract states 'It is only when n becomes larger than a model-dependent threshold that overfitting disappears at infinite training times.' But Section 3 says 'For n > n^*(p) = p, although some overfitting remains (i.e., L_gen > 0), the value of L_gen is sensibly reduced, and the model is no longer expressive enough to memorize.' Thus the abstract overstates the theoretical result: overfitting does not disappear, it remains but is reduced.

E_score is defined as (1/d) E_{x∼P_x} ||s_A(x) − ∇ log P_x||^2, and called the distance to the exact score. But the training loss (3)-(4) targets the score of the noised distribution P_t, not the clean-data score ∇ log P_x. For fixed t>0, the exact reference score is ∇ log P_t(x_t), not ∇ log P_x(x). As written, E_score does not measure the distance to the score being learned, so Fig. 5A is not measuring the quantity claimed.

The text states 'training timescales are directly related to eigenvalues λ via the relation τ^{-1} = ψ_p/(Δ_t λ_min).' But the same text and the immediately following discussion define τ_mem = ψ_p/(Δ_t λ_min), i.e., a time, not a rate. The correct relation is τ = ψ_p/(Δ_t λ_min), or equivalently τ^{-1} = Δ_t λ_min/ψ_p. The equation as printed equates an inverse time to a time.

The memorization criterion is written 'a generated sample x_τ is considered memorized if E_{x_τ}[ ||x_τ − a^{μ1}||_2 / ||x_τ − a^{μ2}||_2 ] < k.' A single generated sample is not an expectation, and f_mem is described as the fraction of generated samples satisfying a per-sample criterion. The formula should define an indicator or probability over generated samples, not an expectation of the ratio being below k.

The paper reports FID curves 'after excluding runs where early stopping failed to improve FID by more than 15%, resulting in reduced variance but biased estimates.' Excluding runs based on the outcome measure that defines τ_gen is a selection-on-outcome procedure and biases the reported generalization window. The admission of bias does not make the protocol valid.

The text says 'τ_max being one to four million SGD steps' and later says 'for n = 32,768, the test loss remains close to the training loss, even after 11 million SGD steps', and later uses 'τ_max = 2M updates' for the n*(p) estimate. These statements imply inconsistent maximum training durations across the same reported experiments.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, 'Memorization is not due to data repetition'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paragraph says alternative experiments 'produce conflicting results, leaving the exact cause of memorization delay open', then immediately concludes 'This confirms that memorization in DMs is driven by a fundamental n-dependent change in the loss landscape—not by sample repetition during training.' This is internally contradictory. It also claims 'even if at fixed τ all models have processed each sample equally often', which is not true under the stated protocol with batch size min(n,512) and fixed SGD steps.

The text says 'we measure for a given τ the largest n(τ) yielding f_mem ≈ 0', but the figure caption and the threshold logic require the smallest n such that f_mem(τ)=0 (or the largest n with f_mem>0). As written, the largest n with f_mem≈0 is simply the largest n tested, not the memorization boundary n(τ).
